newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Scandal hits Hong Kong over immigration boss.
newsitem.headline: Scandal hits Hong Kong over immigration boss.

text.p: A scandal over the shock resignation last July of Hong Kong's immigration chief grew on Wednesday as the government linked his departure to a graft probe that uncovered misconduct.

The government's personnel chief Lam Woon-kwong appeared at a Legislative Council inquiry to say the government had lost confidence in Immigration Director Laurence Leung's personal integrity and discipline before he stepped down last July.
Lam said the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) investigated Leung "to determine whether or not offences under the Bribery Ordinance had been committed".
He said the probe failed to substantiate suspicions of criminal offences but raised grave questions about Leung's integrity. He said Hong Kong's security was not affected,
"The ICAC investigation has uncovered information which causes us to have great doubt on Mr Leung's suitability to remain in the service," Lam said.
He also read out at the inquiry a draft letter written months ago mentioning disciplinary questions and noting Leung used a government housing loan to buy property in Canada.
Lam's unprecedented statement came after months of intense pressure and conspiracy theories from politicians and the media, and allegations of a cover-up.
Lam's statement marked a U-turn in the government's public stance on the case. Leung and the government initially said he retired for "personal reasons".
But Leung, testifying at the inquiry last week, backtracked and said he had been forced to resign.

Leung, 55, who spent seven years as head of immigration and 31 years in the Civil Service, held a highly sensitive post, with strong security implications in the delicate period running up to China's takeover of the British colony on July 1.
He was responsible for areas such as the issuing of passports and visas, immigration and border controls and was privy to sensitive information in handover talks with China.

Lam, the Secretary for the Civil Service, told the Legislative Council's Select Committee inquiry panel that the case was discussed "at the highest level", indicating that British colonial Governor Chris Patten, who is currently in London, was involved in handling the problem.
He said the government had decided it could apply to Leung its Colonial Regulation 59 (CR59) enabling the government to force the early retirement of officials for misconduct.
But Lam said Hong Kong's security had not been compromised by any of Leung's misconduct.
"There is no evidence to suggest that the security and integrity of any systems for which the Immigration Department is responsible has been compromised," Lam told the panel.
"The issue that concerns us here is the personal integrity of the head of an important disciplinary service," he said.

"The fact is that Mr Leung chose to retire voluntarily and with immediate effect. It is equally a fact that Mr Leung chose not to face CR59 proceedings," Lam said, adding that he would like to know why Leung took this course of action.
Lam gave the inquiry a copy of the draft letter which would have been used to apply the CR59 procedure.
The letter, which Lam read out aloud, asked Leung to consider retiring "in the public interest" on grounds that "we have lost confidence in your integrity" after a bribery probe.
The letter alleged misconduct in Leung's use of a HK$1.76 million (US$228,000) government housing loan for the purchase of a property in Canada.
"You subsequently sold the property in 1991 but you failed to report the sale of the property to the Civil Service in accordance with Civil Service regulations," the letter said.
It also said Leung had broken rules covering repayment of the loan.

The letter accused Leung of breaking disciplinary rules on disclosure of investments by officials. It listed interests which Leung held in several companies, one of which involved a local legislator "with whom an officer in your position would inevitably have official dealings from time to time".
"The incidents outlined above have cast grave doubt on your personality, integrity and judgement as a senior government officer," the letter said. (US$1 = HK$7.73)
